rows.speaker: واثلة بن الأسقع
rows.claim: Wathila reports from the Prophet that Abraham’s scrolls began on Ramadan’s first night, the Torah on day six, the Gospel on day thirteen, and the Qur’an on day twenty-four.
rows.anchor: وروى واثلة بن الأسقع عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال: «أنزلت صحف إبراهيم في أول ليلة

rows.speaker: أبو ذر
rows.claim: A report from Abu Dharr dates Abraham’s scrolls to Ramadan day three and Jesus’s Gospel to day eighteen.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية أبي ذر: «نزلت صحف إبراهيم في ثلاث مضين من رمضان، وإنجيل عيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reconciles the dates by taking Wathila’s report to describe the beginning of revelation and Abu Dharr’s to describe its completion.
rows.anchor: والجمع بين الروايتين بأن رواية واثلة أخبر فيها عن ابتداء نزول الصحف والإنجيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers explaining Ibn Kathir’s reading of al-Qurʾān as transferring the hamza vowel to the rāʾ and dropping the hamza throughout the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير القران بنقل حركة الهمزة إلى الراء، وحذف الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative derivation treats the unhamzated nūn in qurʾān as original, from qarana, meaning to join one thing to another.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم قول من قال: إن النون فيه مع عدم الهمز أصلية من قرنت الشيء في الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hudan is an accusative circumstantial verbal noun functioning as hādiyan; it describes the Qurʾān, with li-l-nās attached to it and anzala as its governor.
rows.anchor: هدى للناس وبينات انتصاب: هدى، على الحال وهو مصدر وضع موضع اسم الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayyināt is another necessary circumstantial description, coordinated with hudan; it specifies the manifest kind of guidance among the Qurʾān’s ambiguous and clear teachings.
rows.anchor: وعطف قوله: وبينات، على: هدى، فهو حال أيضا، وهي لازمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase from guidance and criterion describes both guidance and clear signs as part of God’s wider guidance and criterion, which include divine scriptures.
rows.anchor: من الهدى والفرقان هذا في موضع الصفة لقوله: هدى وبينات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-furqān conveys that clear signs distinguish truth from falsehood, and its sound also echoes the preceding verse-endings, making it apt in meaning and cadence.
rows.anchor: ولأن في لفظ: الفرقان، مؤاخاة للفاصلة قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the claim that guidance and criterion here mean the Qurʾān itself, since that would make the Qurʾān part of itself.
rows.anchor: ولا يظهر هنا ما قاله بعض الناس من أن الهدى والفرقان أريد به القرآن

rows.speaker: المنتخب
rows.claim: Al-Muntakhab allows the first guidance to mean principles of religion and the second to mean its branches.
rows.anchor: وفي (المنتخب) أنه يحتمل أن يحمل: هدى الأول على أصول الدين، والثاني على فروعه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya takes the definite article in al-hudā as anaphoric, pointing back to the first, indefinite hudan.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: اللام في الهدى للعهد، والمراد الأول.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He argues Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s anaphoric reading fails under the syntax: attaching min al-hudā to hudan or bayyināt would make the description part of, or self-specifying for, its referent.
rows.anchor: لا جائز أن يكون صفة لهدى، لأنه من حيث هو وصف لزم أن يكون بعضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also rejects attaching min al-hudā to bayyināt, since bayyināt is coordinated as a circumstantial description and would then restrict the Qurʾān through hudan and itself.
rows.anchor: ولا جائز أن يكون صفة لبينات فقط، لأن وبينات معطوف على هدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He therefore reads hudan and furqān as general categories of divine guidance and criterion, of which this Qurʾān is one part.
rows.anchor: فلذلك اخترنا أن يكون الهدى والفرقان عامين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-shahr refers anaphorically to Ramadan; it could have been replaced by a pronoun, but is stated explicitly for honor and emphasis.
rows.anchor: الألف واللام في الشهر للعهد، ويعني به شهر رمضان، ولذلك ينوب عنه الضمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Witnessing the month means being present in it; al-shahr is an adverbial of time, and a legally responsible resident must fast because the imperative requires obligation.
rows.anchor: ومعنى شهود الشهر الحضور فيه. فانتصاب الشهر على الظرف، والمعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians also parse al-shahr as an object with an omitted complement, meaning the town or region witnessed.
rows.anchor: وقالوا على انتصاب الشهر: أنه مفعول به، وهو على حذف مضاف

rows.speaker: علي، ابن عباس، عبيدة المسلماني، النخعي، السدي
rows.claim: This group says one who entered Ramadan while resident must complete its fast even if later traveling; only someone already traveling at its entry may break the fast.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا ذهب علي، وابن عباس، وعبيدة المسلماني، والنخعي، والسدي.

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority say whoever witnesses the month’s beginning or end fasts for as long as resident.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على أن من شهد أول الشهر أو آخره فليصم ما دام مقيما

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī insists al-shahr and its pronoun are adverbial, since both resident and traveler witness the month.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: الشهر منصوب على الظرف، وكذلك الهاء في: فليصمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He answers that an object reading remains possible if the omitted object is dukhūl al-shahr, entry into the month.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم أن ذلك يكون على حذف مضاف تقديره: فمن شهد منكم دخول الشهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He calls the proposed ellipsis “the crescent of the month” weak: Arabic uses shāhada rather than shahida for seeing the crescent, and that reading would wrongly oblige everyone who saw it.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التقدير هلال الشهر، وهذا ضعيف، لأنك لا تقول: شهدت الهلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He finds Abū al-Baqāʾ’s parsing of minkum both as a circumstantial phrase and as governed directly by shahida contradictory.
rows.anchor: فتناقض، لأن جعلها حالا يوجب أن يكون العامل محذوفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Man in man shahida may be either conditional or relative, as in earlier parallels.
rows.anchor: ومن، من قوله فمن شهد، الظاهر أنها شرطية، ويجوز أن تكون موصولة

rows.speaker: الكسائي والفراء
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ say Arabic sometimes uses the purpose lām where an is expected after arāda and amara.
rows.anchor: بل ذلك مذهب الكسائي والفراء، زعما أن العرب تجعل لام كي في موضع أن

rows.speaker: سيبويه وأصحابه
rows.claim: Sībawayh and his associates keep the lām in its ordinary sense and posit an elided an after it, with the preceding verb construed as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وذهب سيبويه وأصحابه إلى أن اللام هنا باقية على حالها وأن مضمرة بعدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians instead call the lām extra; he refers readers to his earlier extended treatment of the issue.
rows.anchor: وذهب بعض الناس إلى زيادة اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says Ibn ʿAṭiyya mislabels the analysis as Basran: treating the lām as the direct-object lām conflicts with also making it part of an elided-an construction.
rows.anchor: وتناقض قول ابن عطية أيضا لأنه قال: هي اللام الداخلة على المفعول

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya proposes that the lām is a command lām and the wāw coordinates one independent clause with another.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن تكون هذه اللام لام الأمر والواو عاطفة جملة كلام على جملة كلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the command-lām analysis: the second-person imperative with an overt address prefix and lām is a rare poor dialect, and no reader is reported to have made this lām vowelless.
rows.anchor: اللغة الأخرى هي الجيدة الفصيحة، وهو، أن يكون الفعل عاريا من حرف المضارعة ومن اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since command lām would be read with the other command-lām forms, the reported reading supports a prepositional, not imperative, lām; the wāw then coordinates phrases rather than clauses.
rows.anchor: فلو كانت لام الأمر لكانت كسائر أخواتها من القراءة بالوجهين فيها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī makes the lām causal and coordinates it with an omitted cause: God wills ease so that people complete the count.
rows.anchor: أحدها: أن تكون الواو عاطفة على علة محذوفة، التقدير: لتعملوا ما تعملون ولتكملوا العدة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ supplies an omitted verb after the wāw: the act was done so that the count would be completed.
rows.anchor: أن يكون بعد الواو فعل محذوف هو المعلل، التقدير: وفعل هذا لتكملوا العدة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj makes it coordinated with an omitted cause whose result is also omitted: God did this to ease matters and to complete the count.
rows.anchor: أن يكون معطوفا على علة محذوفة وقد حذف معلولها، التقدير: فعل الله ذلك ليسهل عليكم ولتكملوا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports a Kūfan view that places the implied causal act after its purpose: the concession was granted so you could complete the count.
rows.anchor: أن يكون الفعل المعلل مقدرا بعد التعليل، تقديره: ولأن تكملوا العدة رخص لكم هذه الرخصة

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: Another proposal treats the wāw as extra, yielding “God wills ease in order to complete the count”; Abū Ḥayyān calls it weak.
rows.anchor: الخامس: أن الواو زائدة، التقدير: يريد الله بكم اليسر لتكملوا العدة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī assigns the implied act “He legislated this” to the whole passage: completing the count, magnifying God, and giving thanks each have a distinct purpose.
rows.anchor: شرع ذلك، يعني جملة ما ذكر من أمر الشاهد بصوم الشهر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He calls this distribution of purposes a subtle rhetorical “folding” construction that only expert critics readily unpack.
rows.anchor: وهذا نوع من اللف لطيف المسلك لا يكاد يهتدي إلى تبيينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article in al-ʿidda most likely refers to make-up days missed in illness or travel, so one fasts an equal number of days later.
rows.anchor: والألف واللام في قوله: ولتكملوا العدة الظاهر أنها للعهد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative takes the count to mean a complete lunar Ramadan, whether it has twenty-nine or thirty days.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عدة الهلال سواء كانت تسعة وعشرين يوما أم كان ثلاثين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in “that you magnify God” is coordinated with the lām in completing the count and has the same grammatical analysis.
rows.anchor: ولتكبروا الله على ما هداكم معطوف على: ولتكملوا العدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takbīr here means magnifying and praising God in any words of praise, not necessarily the formula Allahu akbar.
rows.anchor: ومعنى التكبير هنا تعظيم الله والثناء عليه، فلا يختص ذلك بلفظ التكبير

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Others take the phrase as the specific takbīr at sighting the Shawwāl crescent; Ibn ʿAbbās says Muslims must magnify God when they see it.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس أنه قال: حق على المسلمين إذا رأوا هلال شوال أن يكبروا

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyān identifies the takbīr with the Eid al-Fiṭr day.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان: هو التكبير يوم الفطر.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says takbīr begins at the crescent and lasts until the sermon ends, pausing when the imam goes out and resuming with him.
rows.anchor: فعن ابن عباس: يكبر من رؤية الهلال إلى انقضاء الخطبة

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī’s reported period runs from sighting the crescent until the imam goes out to prayer.
rows.anchor: وقيل: وهو قول الشافعي: من رؤية الهلال إلى خروج الإمام إلى الصلاة

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم ومالك
rows.claim: Zayd b. Aslam and Mālik begin takbīr when a person leaves home and continue until the imam goes out.
rows.anchor: وقال زيد بن أسلم، ومالك: من حين يخرج من منزله إلى أن يخرج الإمام

rows.speaker: ابن القاسم وعلي بن زياد
rows.claim: They distinguish departure before versus after sunrise: an early departure waits until sunrise, while a later one includes takbīr en route and while waiting for the imam.
rows.anchor: وروى ابن القاسم، وعلي بن زياد: إن خرج قبل طلوع الشمس فلا يكبر

rows.speaker: أحمد
rows.claim: Reports from Aḥmad differ on when takbīr stops at the prayer ground; Abū Yaʿlā reads one report as ending when the imam appears, while Ḥanbal says it ends after the sermon.
rows.anchor: واختلف عن أحمد، فنقل الأثر عنه أنه إذا جاء إلى المصلى يقطع

rows.speaker: مالك، الشافعي، أحمد، أبو يوسف، محمد
rows.claim: Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Abū Yūsuf, and Muḥammad treat Eid al-Aḍḥā and Eid al-Fiṭr alike for takbīr; Abū Ḥanīfa restricts it to Aḍḥā.
rows.anchor: فقال مالك، والشافعي، وأحمد، وأبو يوسف، ومحمد: الفطر والأضحى سواء

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority say the formula is Allahu akbar three times, a form transmitted from Jābir; other formulas add tahlīl, tasbīḥ, or praise.
rows.anchor: وكيفيته عند الجمهور: الله أكبر الله أكبر الله أكبر، ثلاثا، وهو مروي عن جابر

rows.speaker: ابن المبارك
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mubārak’s formula adds the testimony of God’s oneness, praise, and gratitude for guidance.
rows.anchor: وكان ابن المبارك يقول: الله أكبر الله أكبر لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mundhir reports that Mālik did not set a fixed limit for the takbīr.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن المنذر: كان مالك لا يجد فيه حدا

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī says his school chose unrestricted takbīr, which he considers the apparent sense of the text; Aḥmad says all forms are acceptable.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن العربي: اختار علماؤنا التكبير المطلق وهو ظاهر الكتاب

rows.speaker: المنتخب
rows.claim: Al-Muntakhab prefers taking completion of the count as Ramadan fasting and magnification as takbīr at its end for guidance to obedience, not generic glorification.
rows.anchor: ورجح في (المنتخب) أن إكمال العدة هو في صوم رمضان

rows.speaker: المنتخب
rows.claim: It argues that general glorification is already required at all times and in every act of worship, so it would not be specially mentioned here.
rows.anchor: لأن تكبير الله بمعنى تعظيمه هو واجب في جميع الأوقات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition ʿalā attached to takabbirū carries a causal implication, as in thanking someone for a favor.
rows.anchor: و: على، تتعلق: بتكبروا، وفيها إشعار بالعلية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains the elevated preposition as takbīr carrying an implied sense of praise: magnify God while praising Him for guiding you.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: وإنما عدى فعل التكبر بحرف الاستعلاء لكونه مضمنًا معنى الحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says al-Zamakhsharī’s wording explains the meaning, not the syntax; syntactically the sense is to praise God through takbīr for His guidance.
rows.anchor: هو تفسير معنى لا تفسير إعراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent reading makes mā a verbal noun, meaning “for your being guided”; reading it as “that which” requires two unlikely omissions.
rows.anchor: والظاهر في: ما، أنها مصدرية أي: على هدايتكم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: If mā is relative, the phrase means guidance to the Islamic law, or guidance away from the Christians’ alteration of fasting.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى، هدايتكم لما ضل فيه النصارى من تبديل صيامهم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya takes “perhaps you will give thanks” as human-oriented hope and thanks for guidance.
rows.anchor: هو ترج في حق البشر على نعمة الله في الهداية، قاله ابن عطية

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation makes the thanks due for the reward God grants for acts of obedience.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى تشكرون على ما أنعم به من ثواب طاعاتكم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He cites the Qurʾānic statement that God is nearer than the jugular and a Prophetic report describing Him as between people and their mounts’ necks.
rows.anchor: ونحن أقرب إليه من حبل الوريد وما روي من قوله عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ in “I am near” answers the conditional; an omitted “say to them” is needed because the consequence is the report of nearness, not nearness itself.
rows.anchor: وثم قول محذوف تقديره: فقل لهم إني قريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “I answer the caller” may describe “near” or be a second predicate; its first-person form follows the preceding first-person expression, as Arabic allows agreement with either antecedent or predicate.
rows.anchor: وروعي الضمير في: فإني، فلذلك جاء أجيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The governing word for idhā is ajību.
rows.anchor: والعامل في: إذا، قوله أجيب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the response clause was revealed after people questioned how God could be near with seven thick heavens between them; it clarifies nearness as answering and power.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه نزل قوله: أجيب دعوة الداع إذا دعان لما نزل: فإني قريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording apparently promises an answer to every caller: both daʿwah and al-dāʿī are generic, and the singular verbal noun does not mean one instance.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله: أجيب دعوة الداع عموم الدعوات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some qualify the promise by God’s will, as stated explicitly in another verse.
rows.anchor: فقيدت الإجابة بمشيئة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other qualifications make the request accord with divine decree, be good for the petitioner, or be possible; the author notes that not every request is granted as asked.
rows.anchor: وقد يثبت بصريح العقل وصحيح النقل أن بعض الدعاة لا يجيبه الله

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: Some restrict the promise to an obedient caller who avoids disobedience.
rows.anchor: فخصصوا الداعي بأن يكون: مطيعا مجتنبا لمعاصيه.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet describes a traveler who raises his hands yet eats, drinks, and wears unlawful things, asking how his prayer could be answered.
rows.anchor: وقد صح أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال في الرجل يطيل السفر: «أشعث أغبر يمد يديه إلى السماء

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A sound report says prayer is answered so long as a person does not become impatient and complain that it has gone unanswered.
rows.anchor: ففي (الصحيح) : يستجاب لأحدكم ما لم يعجل

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd reports the Prophet’s teaching that a sinless, non-severing supplication receives one of three outcomes: immediate grant, deferred reward, or equivalent protection from harm.
rows.anchor: ففي الصحيح عن أبي سعيد قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «ما من مسلم يدعوه بدعوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supplication should use transmitted wording, avoid contrived pre-Islamic rhyming prose, and be grammatically correct.
rows.anchor: وينبغي أن يكون الدعاء بالمأثور، وأن لا يقصد فيه السجع، سجع الجاهلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He lists hoped-for times and places for answered prayer, including dawn, the last third of night, breaking the fast, between calls, distress, rain, battle, Eid, the Friday hour, the Kaʿba, the Prophet’s chamber, and al-Aqṣā.
rows.anchor: وترتجى الإجابة من الأزمان عند السحر، وفي الثلث الأخير من الليل، ووقت الفطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A caller with the stated qualities may expect an answer, but others must not despair; the text cites the prohibition on despairing from God’s mercy.
rows.anchor: فإن الله تعالى قال: قل يا عبادي الذين أسرفوا على أنفسهم لا تقنطوا من رحمة الله

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: Sufyān b. ʿUyayna says people should not stop praying because of their faults, since God answered even Iblīs’s request to be reprieved.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان بن عيينة: لا يمنعن أحد من الدعاء ما يعلم من نفسه

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila restrict answered prayer as a praiseworthy description to believers who have not mixed faith with wrongdoing; a sinner may get what he asked for without that being called an answer.
rows.anchor: وقالت المعتزلة: الإجابة مختصة بالمؤمنين الذين آمنوا ولم يلبسوا إيمانهم بظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer is a supreme act of servitude because it displays dependence on God; revelation and the prophets command and practice it, refuting those who say it has no benefit.
rows.anchor: قيل: والدعاء أعظم مقامات العبودية لأنه إظهار الافتقار إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: قائلون ممن يسمون علماء الحقيقة
rows.claim: One group says prayer is appropriate for afterlife matters but unnecessary for worldly needs because God already undertakes them.
rows.anchor: يستحب الدعاء فيما يتعلق بأمور الآخرة، وأما ما يتعلق بأمور الدنيا فالله متكفل

rows.speaker: قائلون منهم
rows.claim: Another group says to pray when the praying state improves the heart and inner self, but to refrain when silence is better.
rows.anchor: إن كان في حالة الدعاء أصلح، وقلبه أطيب، وسره أصفى، ونفسه أزكى

rows.speaker: قائلون منهم
rows.claim: Some say always to leave prayer as a sign of trust, non-objection, and surrender of choice.
rows.anchor: ترك الدعاء في كل حال أصلح لما فيه من الثقة بالله

rows.speaker: قائلون منهم
rows.claim: Some say abandoning sins itself functions as prayer, since God then takes charge of one’s affairs.
rows.anchor: ترك الذنوب هو الدعاء لأنه إذا تركها تولى الله أمره

rows.speaker: مؤولون
rows.claim: One interpretation makes supplication the profession of divine unity and praise, and response God’s acceptance of that confession.
rows.anchor: أن يكون الدعاء عبارة عن التوحيد والثناء على الله

rows.speaker: مؤولون
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes response to mean hearing: “I hear.”
rows.anchor: الوجه الثاني: أن الإجابة هو السماع فكأنه قال: أسمع

rows.speaker: مؤولون
rows.claim: A third reading makes supplication repentance and response acceptance of repentance.
rows.anchor: الوجه الثالث: أن الدعاء هو التوبة عن الذنوب لأن التائب يدعو الله عند التوبة

rows.speaker: مؤولون
rows.claim: A fourth reading equates supplication with worship and response with fulfillment of the promised reward; it cites the verse’s pairing of “call upon Me” with “worship.”
rows.anchor: الوجه الرابع: أن يكون الدعاء هو العبادة، وفي الحديث: «الدعاء العبادة»

rows.speaker: مؤولون
rows.claim: A fifth interpretation says response may mean either granting or withholding what was requested, with God choosing what is better; Abū Ḥayyān says all these interpretations depart from the apparent sense.
rows.anchor: الوجه الخامس: الإجابة أعم من أن يكون بإعطاء المسئول وبمنعه، فالمعنى

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab reads fastajībū lī as asking God to answer them; here the derived form means request.
rows.anchor: قاله ثعلب، فيكون: استفعل، قد جاءت بمعنى الطلب

rows.speaker: مجاهد، أبو عبيدة وغيرهما
rows.claim: Mujāhid, Abū ʿUbayda, and others read it as answering God’s call to faith and obedience just as He answers people’s needs; istifʿāl here functions like the basic verb.
rows.anchor: قاله مجاهد، وأبو عبيدة، وغيرهما. ويكون:

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء الخراساني
rows.claim: Abū Rajāʾ al-Khurāsānī glosses it as praying to God.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو رجاء الخراساني: معناه فليدعوا لي

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says it means to yield to the call.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش: فليذعنوا الإجابة

rows.speaker: مجاهد والربيع
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Rabīʿ gloss it as obeying.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد أيضا، والربيع: فليطيعوا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes response as talbiya, the pilgrim’s formula “labbayk Allāhumma labbayk”; the lām is a command lām and is not reported read with kasra.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الاستجابة هنا التلبية، وهو: لبيك اللهم لبيك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to believe is not a new conversion, since the passage addresses believers; it instead calls for lasting faith, sincerity, or belief in God’s promised answer.
rows.anchor: وحمله على الأمر بإنشاء الإيمان فيه بعد لأن صدر الآية يقتضي أنهم مؤمنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read yarshudūn actively; other transmitted readings make it passive or vary the vowels, with differing reports for Abū Ḥaywa and Ibrāhīm b. Abī ʿAbla.
rows.anchor: قراءة الجمهور بفتح الياء وضم الشين، وقرأ قوم: يرشدون مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Responding to and believing in God gives people hope of guidance toward what benefits their religion and worldly life; the obligation serves their welfare, not God’s interests.
rows.anchor: وآمنوا به كانوا على رجاء من حصول الرشد لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the Qurʾān depicts faith as a traversed path, it fittingly closes with guidance, as in the prayer for the straight path.
rows.anchor: ولما كان الإيمان شبه بالطريق المسلوك في القرآن، ناسب ذكر الرشاد وهو: الهداية

rows.speaker: البراء
rows.claim: Al-Barāʾ reports that after Ramadan fasting was prescribed, men who had wronged themselves through nighttime eating or intercourse prompted this verse; some had been allowed those acts only until sleeping or the night prayer.
rows.anchor: رواه البخاري، عن البراء: لما نزل صوم رمضان كله، وكان رجال يخونون أنفسهم، فنزلت،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says ʿUmar, Kaʿb al-Anṣārī, and others had intercourse after the night prayer, while Qays b. Ṣirma slept before eating, fasted, and fainted; the verse then descended.
rows.anchor: وأن عمر، وكعبا الأنصاري، وجماعة من الصحابة واقعوا أهلهم بعد العشاء الآخرة

rows.speaker: بعض العلماء
rows.claim: Some scholars say a single lapse occasioned the verse, which became a concession for all Muslims until the end of time.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض العلماء: نزلت الآية في زلة ندرت، فجعل ذلك سبب رخصة لجميع المسلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage completes the rules for circumstances faced by a fasting person and eases the earlier comparison with prior communities, whose fast forbade food, drink, and intercourse after sleep or night prayer.
rows.anchor: ومناسبة هذه الآية لما قبلها من الآيات أنها من تمام الأحوال التي تعرض للصائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Permitting these acts from the start of night until dawn was kindness to Muslims and fulfills the preceding promise that God wills ease, not hardship.
rows.anchor: وناسب أيضا قوله تعالى: في آخر آية الصوم: يريد الله بكم اليسر ولا يريد بكم العسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb “was made lawful” implies prior prohibition, though intercourse and food had still been lawful early in the night before sleeping or the night prayer.
rows.anchor: وقوله: أحل، يقتضي أنه كان حراما قبل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read uḥilla passively with its agent omitted; an active reading makes God the understood agent or shifts from first to third person.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: أحل، مبنيا للمفعول، وحذف الفاعل للعلم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laylat is grammatically an adverb but semantically gives the time of rafath; its syntactic governor is implicit because a verbal noun cannot front its complement under the stricter analysis.
rows.anchor: وانتصاب: ليلة، على الظرف، ولا يراد بليلة الوحدة بل الجنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive “night of fasting” is licensed by loose association: fasting is intended at night and becomes actual during part of the night-to-day cycle.
rows.anchor: وأضيفت: الليلة، إلى الصيام على سبيل الاتساع

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh reads rafath as rafūth.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: الرفث، وقرأ عبد الله: الرفوث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rafath euphemistically means intercourse; the word can name explicit sexual speech, and its shameful closeness to a vulgar term rebukes those who violated the earlier ban.
rows.anchor: وكنى به هنا عن الجماع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition ilā is used because rafath is construed with the sense of ifḍāʾ, intimate access; this yields a discreet Qurʾānic euphemism.
rows.anchor: وعدي بإلى، وإن كان أصله التعدية بالباء لتضمينه معنى الإفضاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-nisāʾ is explained either as the plural of niswah or as a non-pattern plural of imraʾah, and is annexed to the addressees to mark wives or owned women as exclusive partners.
rows.anchor: وأضاف: النساء إلى المخاطبين لأجل الاختصاص، إذ لا يحل الإفضاء إلا لمن اختصت بالمفضي

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says a woman is a man’s clothing, bedding, and waist-wrap because of the closeness and intermingling between them.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: يقال للمرأة هي لباسك، وفراشك، وإزارك لما بينهما

rows.speaker: الربيع
rows.claim: Al-Rabīʿ glosses the spouses as each other’s quilt.
rows.anchor: قال الربيع: هن لحاف لكم وأنتم لحاف لهن

rows.speaker: مجاهد والسدي
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Suddī read the spouses as mutual comfort and repose.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد، والسدي: هن سكن لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clothing sentence is independent explanatory prose, showing why intercourse was permitted: spouses cannot endure separation because they intermingle like garments.
rows.anchor: وهذه الجملة لا موضع لها من الإعراب، بل هي مستأنفة كالبيان لسبب الإحلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse mentions women as clothing first because it portrays men’s greater need and lesser patience, and the man as usually initiating intimacy.
rows.anchor: وقدم: هن لباس لكم، على قوله: وأنتم لباس لهن، لظهور احتياج الرجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He identifies three rhetorical devices: semantic antithesis in making lawful what was previously forbidden, euphemism in rafath, and a striking clothing metaphor.
rows.anchor: جمعت الآية ثلاثة أنواع من البيان: الطباق المعنوي، بقوله: أحل لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Libās is singular because it functions like a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وأفرد اللباس لأنه كالمصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax of ʿalima annakum varies by whether ʿalima is construed like “know” or in its original two-object construction; takhtānū is iftiʿāl with the sense of khānū.
rows.anchor: وتختانون: هو من الخيانة، وافتعل هنا بمعنى فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ikhtiyān may intensify betrayal: intercourse or eating after sleeping violated the rule and harmed the offenders’ own prospects for good.
rows.anchor: والاختيان هنا معبر به عما وقعوا فيه من المعصية بالجماع

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other glosses say they selfishly reserved forbidden pleasures for themselves, or took care of themselves by approaching their wives; takhawwana can mean to care for, with n replacing the more usual l.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه، تستأثرون أنفسكم فيما نهيتم عنه

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim reads the phrase as failing to give the self its due, explaining why it says “yourselves” rather than “God.”
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مسلم: هي عبارة عن عدم الوفاء بما يجب عليه من حق النفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He takes the betrayal as an actual past lapse, indicated by kāna and sound transmission; the hypothetical reading is weak because it lacks support and conflicts with “He turned toward you.”
rows.anchor: وظاهر الكلام وقوع الخيانة منهم لدلالة كان على ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He turned toward you” means He accepted their repentance after the forbidden acts; some instead understand it as easing the rule and granting permission.
rows.anchor: أي: قبل توبتكم حين تبتم مما ارتكبتم من المحظور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He pardoned you” means He forgave the sins and will not punish them; one report says repentance erases sin and pardon erases its trace, so the paired verbs intensify one sense.
rows.anchor: وعفا عنكم أي: عن ذنوبكم فلا يؤاخذكم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another gloss takes pardon as leaving the prohibition behind or making the matter easy, as when something is said to be waived.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى سهل عليكم أمر النساء فيما يؤتنف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ān means “at this time, this night”; bashirūhunna is a permission command because it follows a prohibition and consensus confirms its permissive sense.
rows.anchor: وهذا أمر يراد به الإباحة لكونه ورد بعد النهي

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority take mubāsharah as intercourse; another view includes intercourse and lesser bodily contact, from the idea of skin-to-skin contact.
rows.anchor: والمباشرة في قول الجمهور: الجماع، وقيل: الجماع فما دونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if mubāsharah here means intercourse, its permission necessarily includes lesser acts.
rows.anchor: وإن قلنا: المراد به هنا الجماع، لقوله: الرفث، ولسبب النزول

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وعكرمة والحسن والضحاك والربيع والسدي والحكم بن عتيبة
rows.claim: Their first interpretation of “seek what God prescribed” is offspring decreed for the spouses; intercourse serves procreation, the purpose of marriage, not pleasure alone.
rows.anchor: أحدها: أنه الولد، قاله ابن عباس، ومجاهد، وعكرمة، والحسن، والضحاك

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic saying urges marriage and procreation, since the Prophet will take pride in the community’s numbers on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: تناكحوا تناسلوا فإني مكاثر بكم الأمم يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A second interpretation is to seek the lawful site of intercourse rather than a prohibited one.
rows.anchor: الثاني: هو محل الوطء أي: ابتغوا المحل المباح الوطء فيه دون ما لم يكتب لكم

rows.speaker: قتادة وابن زيد
rows.claim: Qatāda and Ibn Zayd say it means seeking the permission and concession granted after the restriction was lifted.
rows.anchor: الثالث: هو ما أباحه بعد الحظر، أي: ابتغوا الرخصة والإباحة، قاله قتادة: وابن زيد

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل، ابن عباس
rows.claim: A fourth view, attributed to Muʿādh and also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, reads it as seeking Laylat al-Qadr; al-Zamakhsharī calls this close to an eccentric interpretation.
rows.anchor: الرابع: وابتغوا ليلة القدر، قاله معاذ بن جبل، وروي عن ابن عباس.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والزجاج
rows.claim: A fifth view from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Zajjāj identifies what God prescribed as the Qurʾān and its commands; a variant reading wa-ttabiʿū supports it.
rows.anchor: الخامس: هو القرآن، قاله ابن عباس، والزجاج. أي: ابتغوا ما أبيح لكم وأمرتم به

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view means the permitted conditions and times for intercourse, excluding menstruation, postpartum bleeding, waiting period, and apostasy.
rows.anchor: السادس: هو الأحوال والأوقات التي أبيح لكم المباشرة فيهن

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies the referent as wives and female slaves.
rows.anchor: السابع: هو الزوجة والمملوكة كما في قوله تعالى: إلا على أزواجهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The phrase has also been read as a prohibition of coitus interruptus with free wives.
rows.anchor: الثامن: أن ذاك نهي عن العزل لأنه في الحرائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kataba may mean made, decreed, or recorded in the Preserved Tablet or Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: وكتب هنا بمعنى: جعل، كقوله: كتب في قلوبهم الإيمان أو بمعنى: قضى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers a reinforcing sense: pursue what God permits, namely intercourse throughout the Ramadan night; al-Aʿmash’s irregular “wa-atū” reading supports it but conflicts with the codex consonantal text.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن هذه الجملة تأكيد لما قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eating and drinking are also permission commands, reopening the three activities that had been forbidden during part of the fasting night until dawn appears.
rows.anchor: وكلوا واشربوا أمر إباحة أيضا، أبيح لهم ثلاثة الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text links permission for intercourse to ʿUmar and others, and permission to eat to Qays b. Ṣirma or another report in the occasion of revelation.
rows.anchor: فإحلال الجماع بسبب عمر وغيره، وإحلال الأكل بسبب صرمة أو غيره

rows.speaker: سهل بن سعد
rows.claim: Sahl b. Saʿd reports that some Companions took the white and black threads literally, tying one of each to a foot until the clarification “of dawn” came.
rows.anchor: روى ذلك سهل بن سعد في نزول هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says a Ramadan year passed between the initial wording and the words “of dawn.”
rows.anchor: وروي أنه كان بين نزول: وكلوا واشربوا حتى يتبين لكم الخيط الأبيض

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says most jurists and theologians who reject delaying clarification until the time of need would not accept the report; those allowing delay say it still conveyed the duty to obey pending clarification.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: ومن لا يجوز تأخير البيان- وهم أكثر الفقهاء والمتكلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says this is abrogation, not delayed clarification: Companions acted on the literal threads until “of dawn” replaced that reading with a figurative comparison.
rows.anchor: وليس هذا عندي من تأخير البيان إلى وقت الحاجة، بل هو من باب النسخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The white thread is the light spreading horizontally at true dawn and the black thread is the remaining darkness; without “of dawn” the expression would be metaphor, while the added phrase marks a simile.
rows.anchor: وصارا ذلك مجازين، شبه بالخيط الأبيض ما يبدو من الفجر المعترض في الأفق

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: When ʿAdī b. Ḥātim misunderstood the comparison as literal threads, the Prophet laughed and said his pillow or nape must be broad, an idiom for dullness.
rows.anchor: فضحك وقال: «إن كان وسادك لعريضا» وروي: «إنك لعريض القفاء»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poet’s “broad nape” line illustrates the idiom that a broad nape signals poor understanding; Arabs call anything fine, long, and threadlike a thread.
rows.anchor: والقفا العريض يستدل به على قلة فطنة الرجل، وقال:

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says the phrase refers to two dawns: a dark horizontal false dawn and a bright dawn that fills the horizon.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: هما فجران: أحدهما يبدو سواد معترضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He identifies the white thread as true, spreading dawn rather than false dawn’s vertical light; dawn first appears fine, then spreads, and fasting begins with its first appearance.
rows.anchor: وقوله: من الفجر، يدل على أنه أريد بالخيط الأبيض الصبح الصادق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the majority practice through the generations and accords with reports from Ibn Masʿūd and Samura b. Jundub.
rows.anchor: هذا مذهب الجمهور، وبه أخذ الناس ومضت عليه الأعصار والأمصار

rows.speaker: عثمان وحذيفة وابن عباس وطلق بن علي وعطاء والأعمش
rows.claim: They hold that fasting begins only once dawn can be distinguished on roads or mountaintops.
rows.anchor: وهذا مروي عن عثمان، وحذيفة وابن عباس، وطلق بن علي، وعطاء، والأعمش

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī reportedly prayed dawn with the people and then said the white thread had now become distinct from the black one.
rows.anchor: وروي عن علي أنه صلى الصبح بالناس ثم قال: الآن تبين الخيط الأبيض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the endpoint is discernibility rather than the first instant of dawn, one who eats or has intercourse while genuinely unsure and later learns dawn had begun owes no make-up fast.
rows.anchor: ثم انكشف أنه كان الفجر قد طلع وصام، أنه لا قضاء لأنه غياه بتبين الفجر للصائم لا بالطلوع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās ate after two observers disagreed about whether dawn had appeared and ruled that he owed no make-up fast.
rows.anchor: فقال اختلفتما، فأكل وبان لا قضاء عليه.

rows.speaker: الثوري وعبيد الله بن الحسن والشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Thawrī, ʿUbayd Allāh b. al-Ḥasan, and al-Shāfiʿī agree that eating amid doubt about dawn requires no make-up; Mālik requires it, and the two positions are reported from Abū Ḥanīfa.
rows.anchor: قال الثوري، وعبيد الله بن الحسن، والشافعي، وقال مالك: إن أكل شاكا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since intercourse remains lawful until dawn is discerned, ritual bathing may be delayed until after dawn; this refutes Abū Hurayra’s view, while al-Ḥasan invalidates the fast of one still in major impurity.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه التغيية أيضا دلالة على جواز المباشرة إلى التبين

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that the Prophet would enter dawn in major impurity after intercourse while fasting.
rows.anchor: وقد روت عائشة أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يصبح جنبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where moonlight, clouds, or location prevent observing the horizon, one must act cautiously and refrain until certain dawn has entered.
rows.anchor: فلو كانت مقمرة أو مغيمة، أو كان في موضع لا يشاهد مطلع الفجر

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says only intercourse, eating, and drinking break the fast; vomiting, enemas, and other cases remain permitted because the text names only those three.
rows.anchor: وذهب أبو مسلم أنه لا فطر إلا بهذه الثلاثة: المباشرة، والأكل، والشرب

rows.speaker: الفقهاء
rows.claim: The jurists say the verse names eating, drinking, and intercourse because people desire them; vomiting and enemas are disliked and nasal medication is rare.
rows.anchor: وأما الفقهاء فقالوا: خصت هذه الثلاثة بالذكر لميل النفس إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first min marks a starting point; the second is partitive because the white thread is the first portion of dawn, though both prepositions can govern the same verb with distinct senses.
rows.anchor: ومن الأولى، هي لابتداء الغاية، قيل: وهي مع ما بعدها في موضع نصب

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: On al-Zajjāj’s two-dawn reading, the second min may be partitive of both threads because fajr denotes a genus containing two dawns.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون للتبعيض للخيطين معا، على قول الزجاج

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another parsing makes min al-fajr a circumstantial or explanatory phrase for the white thread, whose clarification suffices to clarify the black thread too.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ويجوز أن يكون من الفجر حالا من الضمير في الأبيض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He explains omission of a matching “from night” after black thread as avoiding awkward repetition and because the black-thread phrase is secondary.
rows.anchor: ولقلق اللفظ لو صرح به، إذ كان: يكون حتى يتبين لكم الخيط الأبيض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fast’s obligation was stated earlier; this verse adds its endpoint, night, which is outside the daytime category, though confirming day’s end entails entry into a portion of night.
rows.anchor: ثم أتموا الصيام إلى الليل: تقدم ذكر وجوب الصوم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the People of the Book fasted from one evening meal to the next, and Muslims were ordered to differ by breaking fast at sunset.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: أهل الكتاب يفطرون من العشاء إلى العشاء، فأمر الله تعالى بالخلاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Completing the fast is obligatory because fasting itself is obligatory; the earlier commands to intercourse, eating, and drinking merely permit what was allowed in principle.
rows.anchor: والأمر بالإتمام هنا للوجوب، لأن الصوم واجب، فإتمامه واجب

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib claims the verse proves daytime intention, allowing ritual bathing to be delayed until dawn, and rejecting continuous fasting.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب: فيه دليل على جواز النية بالنهار، وعلى جواز تأخير الغسل إلى الفجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says daytime intention does not follow: the text commands completing an already begun fast, and its indication of delayed bathing comes from the prior discussion instead.
rows.anchor: أما كون الآية تدل على جواز النية بالنهار فليس بظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The endpoint at night does not by itself refute voluntary continuation; the Prophetic prohibition of wisāl is read by some as forbidden and by others as disliked.
rows.anchor: وأما الدلالة على نفي صوم الوصال، فليس بظاهر، لأنه غيا وجوب إتمام الصوم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير وإبراهيم التيمي وأبو الحوراء
rows.claim: These early Muslims are reported to have practiced continuous fasting; Aḥmad, Isḥāq, and Ibn Wahb allowed it until dawn.
rows.anchor: وقد روي الوصال عن جماعة من الصحابة والتابعين، كعبد الله بن الزبير

rows.speaker: الجمهور وأبو حنيفة والشافعي
rows.claim: If someone mistakenly breaks the fast thinking sunset has occurred and then sees the sun, the majority, Abū Ḥanīfa, and al-Shāfiʿī require make-up but no expiation.
rows.anchor: فلو ظن أن الشمس غربت فأفطر ثم طلعت الشمس فهذا ما أتم إلى الليل

rows.speaker: إسحاق وأهل الظاهر
rows.claim: Isḥāq and the literalists say there is no make-up in that case, analogizing it to forgetfulness; this is also reported from ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وقال إسحاق وأهل الظاهر: لا قضاء عليه كالناسي وروي ذلك عن عمر

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik requires both make-up and expiation when a person breaks the fast while uncertain about sunset; another reported position requires make-up alone by analogy with doubt at dawn.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك: من أفطر شاكا في الغروب قضى وكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sexual intercourse that intentionally breaks the fast entails make-up by consensus; eating or drinking entails make-up for al-Shāfiʿī and make-up plus expiation for other jurists.
rows.anchor: فلو قطع الإتمام متعمدا لجماع، فالإجماع على وجوب القضاء

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority treat forgetful intercourse like deliberate intercourse, though al-Shāfiʿī’s expiation ruling differs; forgetful eating or drinking leaves the fast intact for Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī, while Mālik requires make-up.
rows.anchor: أو ناسيا بجماع فكالمتعمد عند الجمهور

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: One who merely resolves to stop fasting without acting remains fasting without make-up according to the majority; Ibn Ḥabīb and the Mudawwana’s report from Mālik require make-up.
rows.anchor: ولو نوى الفطر بالنهار ولم يفعل، بل رفع نية الصوم، فهو على صومه عند الجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording apparently commands completion only of a fast already begun; although the Sunna separately requires a healthy person who began the day without fasting to abstain.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الآية يقتضي أن الإتمام لا يجب إلا على من تقدم له الصوم

rows.speaker: الحنفية
rows.claim: The Ḥanafīs include voluntary fasting under the general command to complete the fast; the Shāfiʿīs restrict it to obligatory fasting because the passage explains its rules.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الآية يقتضي وجوب إتمام الصوم النفل على ما ذهبت إليه الحنفية

rows.speaker: بعض أرباب الحقائق
rows.claim: A mystical allegory divides Ramadan between God’s due, completing the fast until night, and human needs, eating and drinking until dawn.
rows.anchor: قال بعض أرباب الحقائق: لما علم تعالى أنه لا بد للعبد من الحظوظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When intercourse was permitted at night, some retreatants left the mosque to have sex and returned after bathing; the verse forbids it during retreat both inside and outside the mosque.
rows.anchor: كانوا إذا كانوا معتكفين ودعت ضرورة أحدهم إلى الجماع خرج إلى امرأته

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group limits the prohibited mubāsharah in retreat to intercourse, following the occasion of revelation and immediate context; the majority include pleasurable contact.
rows.anchor: وسبب النزول أن المباشرة هي الجماع فقط، وقال بذلك فرقة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: There is consensus that the prohibition is categorical and intercourse invalidates retreat; schools differ on whether lustful looking, touch, or kissing also invalidates it.
rows.anchor: وانعقد الإجماع على أن هذا النهي نهي تحريم، وأن الاعتكاف يبطل بالجماع

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik says lustful looking, touching, or kissing invalidates retreat; Abū Ḥanīfa conditions invalidation on ejaculation.
rows.anchor: وأما دواعي النكاح: كالنظرة واللمس والقبلة بشهوة فيفسد به الاعتكاف عند مالك

rows.speaker: المزني عن الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Muzanī transmits from al-Shāfiʿī that such an act invalidates retreat if it would produce a comparable legal consequence with an unrelated woman.
rows.anchor: وقال المزني عن الشافعي: إن فعل فسد

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that she combed the Prophet’s head while he was in retreat in the mosque; scholars infer that nonlustful touch is allowed.
rows.anchor: وصح في الحديث أن عائشة كانت ترجل رأس رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وهو معتكف في المسجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If mubāsharah here included mere touching, intercourse would be prohibited a fortiori because it contains touching and more; the touching at issue is understood with desire.
rows.anchor: وكانت المباشرة المعني بها اللمس مقيدة بالشهوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In law, iʿtikāf means restraining oneself in a place for worship and nearness to God, and is an ancient religious practice.
rows.anchor: والعكوف في الشرع عبارة عن حبس النفس في مكان للعبادة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda reads ʿākifūn without the alif, and the clause is a circumstantial phrase meaning “do not approach them while in this state.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ قتادة: وأنتم عكفون، بغير ألف، والجملة في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Retreat is permissible and not obligatory by consensus; the Prophet practiced it, making it a Sunna, though this verse does not specify its recommendation.
rows.anchor: والإجماع على أنه ليس بواجب، وثبت أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم اعتكف، فهو سنة

rows.speaker: علي وابن عمر وابن عباس وعائشة وأبو حنيفة وأصحابه ومالك والثوري والحسن بن صالح
rows.claim: These authorities require fasting as a condition of retreat; a report from ʿĀʾisha calls fasting a Sunna of the retreatant.
rows.anchor: وشرطه الصوم، وهو مروي عن علي، وابن عمر، وابن عباس، وعائشة

rows.speaker: سعيد وإبراهيم وطاووس عن ابن عباس والشافعي
rows.claim: These authorities say fasting is not a condition for retreat.
rows.anchor: وقال جماعة من التابعين، منهم سعيد، وإبراهيم: ليس الصوم شرطا

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī says any duration that counts as remaining in place qualifies as retreat; Mālik’s well-known minimum is ten days, with a report of one day and night.
rows.anchor: وهو مذهب الشافعي. وقال مالك: لا يعتكف أقل من عشرة أيام

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī allows retreat by night, day, or either alone, including a vow for only one night or one day.
rows.anchor: وظاهر إطلاق العكوف أيضا يقتضي جواز اعتكاف الليل والنهار

rows.speaker: سحنون وأبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Sahnūn says a vow of one night is not binding; Abū Ḥanīfa says a vow of days includes their nights.
rows.anchor: وقال سحنون: لو نذر اعتكاف ليلة لم يلزمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “in the mosques” does not establish that a mosque is a condition of retreat: a restriction on intercourse during a state does not define where that state may occur.
rows.anchor: أنه ليس من شرط الاعتكاف كونه في المساجد

rows.speaker: أبو قلابة وابن عيينة والشافعي وداود الطبري وابن المنذر
rows.claim: They say retreat may take place in any mosque, a view also attributed to one opinion of Mālik.
rows.anchor: وبه قال أبو قلابة، وابن عيينة، والشافعي، وداود الطبري، وابن المنذر

rows.speaker: عبد الله وعائشة وإبراهيم وابن جبير وعروة وأبو جعفر
rows.claim: They restrict retreat to a mosque where congregational prayer is held; this is another opinion of Mālik.
rows.anchor: والقول الآخر: أنه لا اعتكاف إلا في مسجد يجمع فيه

rows.speaker: عبد الله وحذيفة
rows.claim: Some say retreat is valid only in one of the three holy mosques; another group limits it to a prophet’s mosque, a position Ibn al-Musayyab holds.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: إنه لا اعتكاف إلا في أحد المساجد الثلاثة

rows.speaker: الحارث عن علي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥārith transmits from ʿAlī that retreat is only valid in the Sacred Mosque or the Prophet’s Mosque.
rows.anchor: وروى الحارث عن علي: أنه لا اعتكاف إلا في المسجد الحرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse expressly addresses men but is silent about women; Abū Ḥanīfa confines a woman to her home mosque, Mālik requires a congregational mosque, and al-Shāfiʿī permits any location.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الآية يدل على جواز الاعتكاف للرجال، وأما النساء فمسكوت عنهن

rows.speaker: مجاهد والأعمش
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Aʿmash read “in the mosque” in the singular; al-Aʿmash means the Sacred Mosque, while the author takes the word generically and favors the plural reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد، والأعمش: في المسجد، على الإفراد

rows.speaker: بعض الصوفية
rows.claim: Some Ṣūfīs say that the place of nearness is sacred and protected from the pursuit of bodily desires.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الصوفية في قوله: ولا تباشروهن الآية.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative plus plural predicate cannot refer only to the single retreat prohibition; “God’s limits” encompasses the whole fasting passage, whose commands also entail prohibitions.
rows.anchor: بل هو إشارة إلى ما تضمنته آية الصيام من أولها إلى هنا

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī glosses God’s limits as His conditions or rules.
rows.anchor: شروطه، قاله السدي. أو: فرائضه، قاله شهر بن حوشب

rows.speaker: شهر بن حوشب
rows.claim: Shahr b. Ḥawshab glosses the limits as God’s obligations.
rows.anchor: أو: فرائضه، قاله شهر بن حوشب.

rows.speaker: الضحاك والزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Zamakhsharī take the limits as sins, sacred prohibitions, or bans.
rows.anchor: أو: معاصيه، قاله الضحاك. وقال معناه الزمخشري

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya understands the limits as the boundaries between permissibility and prohibition.
rows.anchor: أو الحواجز هي الإباحة والحظر قاله ابن عطية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ascribing the limits to God emphasizes that they must not be confused; the phrase is neither indefinite nor marked by the definite article.
rows.anchor: وإضافة الحدود إلى الله تعالى هنا، وحيث ذكرت، تدل على المبالغة في عدم الالتباس بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forbidding people to approach a limit is stronger than merely forbidding transgression, fitting a passage focused on prohibitions.
rows.anchor: النهي عن القربان للحدود أبلغ من النهي عن الالتباس بها

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet compares God’s prohibitions to a king’s protected pasture: one who grazes near the boundary may soon enter it.
rows.anchor: قال صلى الله عليه وسلم: «إن لكل ملك حمى، وحمى الله محارمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The choice of “do not approach” suits a prohibition: elsewhere “do not transgress” follows divorce rules, while “transgress His limits” follows inheritance and family-law allocations, so each wording fits its context.
rows.anchor: وجاء هنا: فلا تقربوها، وفي مكان آخر: فلا تعتدوها

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim reads “do not approach them” as forbidding alteration of the limits, by analogy with the ban on approaching an orphan’s property except in the best manner.
rows.anchor: لا تتعرضوا لها بالتغيير، كقوله: ولا تقربوا مال اليتيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In this way God makes His signs clear” means that, with brief eloquent wording, He explains fasting laws and other revealed legislation so people may be mindful.
rows.anchor: كذلك يبين الله آياته أي: مثل ذلك البيان الذي سبق ذكره في ذكر أحكام الصوم

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim takes God’s signs to mean the obligations He has explained, so people may obey what He revealed; this requires treating the kāf as extra.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مسلم: المراد بالآيات: الفرائض التي بينها، كأنه قال كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He objects that Abū Muslim’s reading works only if the kāf is redundant; if it marks comparison, there must be both a comparator and a compared object.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا يتأتى إلا على اعتقاد أن تكون الكاف زائدة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya restricts “for people” to those whom God enables to receive guidance, citing verses about God’s leading astray.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: معناه خصوص فيمن يسره الله للهدى، بدلالة الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He sees no need for that restriction: God clarifies the signs to all people, but clear presentation does not mean everyone actually understands them.
rows.anchor: ولا حاجة إلى دعوى الخصوص، بل الله تعالى يبين آياته للناس ويوضحها لهم
